From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel — buyer review

## Overall assessment

The Seller’s draft transfers too much risk to Wattlebridge. In particular, it asks the Buyer to complete before key customer and financing risks are resolved, rely on broad data-room disclosure, and accept a liability regime that could restrict remedies for matters far beyond ordinary business warranties.

The Seller’s statements that terms are “standard,” “final” or agreed at principal level are **not evidence of a binding commercial agreement**. We should check the deal record, but independently negotiate the protections needed. The `[STANDARD]` labels do not justify excluding those provisions from review.

Our priority should be to resolve the Bluefen consent and Riverlark debt **before or at Completion**, protect the debt-free/cash-free price against seller-related costs, and obtain targeted protection for Ironquay and the export incident.

## Material issues and proposed pushback

### 1. Bluefen: consent is not yet secured

Bluefen represents approximately **$3.6 million, or 30%, of FY26 revenue**. DD-002 identifies a change-control consent and associated conditions, but the disclosure letter confirms that neither final written consent nor evidence of satisfaction of the conditions has been provided. Loss or impairment of that relationship could materially affect the value of the business.

**Push for:**

- A condition precedent requiring a final, valid written consent **and satisfaction or waiver of all applicable conditions**, on terms acceptable to the Buyer and without adverse amendments, fees or concessions unless the Buyer agrees.
- Seller responsibility for obtaining it, with cooperation, progress reporting and prompt delivery of correspondence.
- A long-stop date and Buyer termination right if it is not satisfied; no unilateral Seller right to deem it satisfied merely by producing a consent.
- Confirmation at Completion that the contract remains in force and no relevant termination right has arisen.

A consent document alone may not resolve the conditions in clause 11.3.

### 2. Riverlark: debt and security must be cleared at Completion

The approximately **$3.2 million** facility is outstanding and no final security discharge is included. A release after Completion is inconsistent with acquiring the business debt-free and would leave the Buyer exposed to a secured lender.

**Push for:**

- A binding lender payout and release arrangement before Completion, with repayment made **simultaneously at Completion** from the Seller’s proceeds.
- A release of all relevant guarantees and security, with registrable discharge documents delivered at Completion or an enforceable lender undertaking and a tightly controlled registration process.
- An express deduction of the full payout, including interest, break costs and fees, under the agreed debt-free/cash-free mechanics, with no double deduction.
- A Completion condition or deliverable preventing the Buyer being required to complete without an effective release arrangement.

### 3. Price mechanics and the $420,000 bonuses

The conditional Completion bonuses do not appear in the funds flow. Whether they crystallise depends on Completion and continued employment; the record does not establish the applicable payroll tax, superannuation or other on-costs. If the Company bears them without adjustment, the Buyer could effectively fund a Seller-side transaction cost.

**Push for:**

- An express allocation to the Seller of the bonuses that crystallise in connection with the sale, **plus applicable employer on-costs**.
- Itemisation in the funds flow and a clear payment or price-adjustment mechanism; reconcile it with debt and working-capital definitions to avoid omission or double counting.
- Confirmation of beneficiaries, conditions, amounts and treatment of employees who leave, supported by the underlying documentation.

Also review the complete completion-accounts and funds-flow provisions: the stated **$24 million debt-free/cash-free price** needs precise definitions of debt, cash and transaction expenses, a consistent adjustment process and appropriate dispute resolution. The supplied extract does not establish that those mechanics work.

### 4. Warranty caps, thresholds and time limits

The proposed general cap is **$4.8 million**; claims must each exceed **$25,000**, and only amounts above an aggregate **$250,000** basket are recoverable. General claims expire after **18 months**. These terms materially reduce recovery even before other limitations apply. Their acceptability depends on the diligence, scope of warranties and overall negotiated package—not the Seller’s unsupported market assertion.

More seriously, applying that regime to **title and capacity** would leave the Buyer potentially paying $24 million for shares the Seller cannot validly transfer, with recovery capped at $4.8 million and subject to a short deadline.

**Push for:**

- A substantially stronger general warranty package: negotiate a higher cap, a lower de minimis and a **tipping basket**—once the basket is crossed, qualifying claims are recoverable from the first dollar.
- Fundamental warranties covering ownership, title, capacity and authority, with a cap up to **100% of price**, no de minimis or basket, and a substantially longer survival period.
- A longer, separately negotiated period for tax claims, aligned with relevant assessment and amendment exposure, and an appropriate tax covenant or indemnity.
- Clear claim-notice provisions: a notice should preserve a claim where it gives reasonable available detail, including for contingent or unquantified loss.

### 5. Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance are too broad

Clauses 9.3, 12.8 and 20.5, together with the proposal that limitations apply to **all claims unless expressly excluded**, could undermine indemnities, tax protection and remedies for deliberate misconduct or other claims. The interaction needs to be controlled expressly; simply negotiating a separate indemnity is insufficient if an overriding limitation catches it.

**Push for:** a precise claims and remedies framework that expressly preserves:

- Claims for **fraud, fraudulent misrepresentation and wilful misconduct**, subject to applicable law.
- Fundamental warranty claims, tax claims and specific indemnities under their **own expressly stated limits and periods**, not the general warranty basket and cap.
- Price adjustments, completion payment obligations, and appropriate rights to specific performance, injunctive relief and other expressly preserved remedies.

Review the entire agreement for conflicting definitions and cross-references. Non-reliance should not inadvertently negate the contractual warranties or any specifically preserved remedies.

### 6. Disclosure and Buyer knowledge could extinguish the protection purchased

The Seller purports to disclose the entire data room, accounts, registers and public records, while barring claims for anything known to the Buyer or its advisers **or discoverable** in the data room or public records. This would shift the burden of identifying and interpreting every possible risk to the Buyer. It could also turn incomplete evidence into a defence: for example, the disclosure letter expressly records unresolved facts about Bluefen, Ironquay and the incident.

**Push for:**

- Disclosure only of matters **fairly disclosed with sufficient detail** to identify their nature and scope and reasonably assess the relevant risk; no blanket disclosure of whole repositories or public records.
- Specific, cross-referenced disclosures against identified warranties, with a fixed, indexed data-room copy.
- Deletion of the “discoverable” knowledge standard. If a knowledge limitation is unavoidable, confine it to actual knowledge of a small named group, without imputation from advisers or constructive knowledge.
- Express preservation of specific indemnities and agreed completion protections regardless of disclosure or Buyer knowledge.

The disclosure letter’s reservation that it does not admit breach or loss does not resolve the underlying risks; nor should disclosure be treated as proof of the outcome.

### 7. Ironquay: potential gap in ownership of project materials

DD-004 makes transfer of SOW3 Project Materials conditional on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 shows **$180,000 open**, but does not independently prove non-payment; no receipt or confirmatory assignment is in the data room. The issue is therefore unresolved, not a proven failure of title. An indemnity limited to the SOW3 payment may not cover the consequences if the Company lacks the rights it needs.

**Push for:**

- Evidence of cleared payment of all SOW3 fees and a confirmatory assignment or other satisfactory direct confirmation of ownership and rights, preferably before Completion.
- A specific indemnity covering loss arising from the matter, including remediation, replacement or licensing costs and third-party claims—not merely the unpaid fee.
- Protection outside the general warranty limitations and disclosure/knowledge defences, with an appropriate separate cap and duration.
- Broader IP warranties addressing ownership or valid rights to use material software and project materials, subject only to fair disclosure.

### 8. Export/privacy incident: investigate and allocate the risk

The link went to an unintended external address and may relate to approximately **1,240 records**. Access, exact scope and notification requirements remain unknown. It is not established to be a confirmed breach, and no loss has been quantified; equally, the Seller’s description as preliminary does not establish immateriality.

**Push for:**

- Prompt preservation of evidence and completion of a documented investigation, including access logs, recipient contact, scope, containment and legal assessment of any notification obligations.
- Buyer access to findings and a controlled process for communications, remediation and cooperation, consistent with legal obligations.
- A tailored indemnity for pre-Completion facts and resulting investigation, remediation and third-party or regulatory costs **to the extent legally recoverable**, with its own negotiated limits and duration, outside general disclosure and warranty thresholds.
- Appropriate data protection and security warranties, with a Completion update if signing and Completion are separated.

### 9. Sandbar renewals: establish the liability before allocating it

Three related renewals total **$330,000**. The disclosures do not establish whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course. We should not assume either that they are Seller debt or that they are harmless future operating costs.

**Push for:** the contracts, renewal and termination dates, notice rights, services and accounting treatment. Allocate any accrued or pre-Completion liability through the agreed debt or working-capital mechanics; address unusual, unavoidable or transaction-triggered commitments separately. Avoid counting the same amount twice.

### 10. Title, lease and Mossvale: verify, but do not overstate

- **Share title:** DD-012 records Harbourglass as holder of all issued shares, but the Buyer has not independently verified the position. Obtain the register and constitutional and corporate records, confirm issued shares and any options, encumbrances or third-party rights, and require executed transfers and other Completion deliverables. Fundamental warranties remain necessary.
- **Office lease:** DD-007 identifies a **notification**, not a consent requirement. Confirm the deadline and responsible party and require the notice and evidence of delivery.
- **Mossvale:** DD-009 restricts assignment; it does **not**, on the stated facts, establish that a share sale needs consent. Review the full contract, including change-control and termination provisions, before requiring consent.

## Recommended negotiation priorities

1. **Completion protections:** Bluefen consent with all conditions satisfied; simultaneous Riverlark payout and security release.
2. **Price protection:** implement debt-free/cash-free mechanics and allocate the conditional bonuses and applicable on-costs; investigate the Sandbar renewals.
3. **Targeted risk protection:** resolve Ironquay ownership and investigate the export incident, supported by appropriately drafted specific indemnities.
4. **Restore meaningful recourse:** separate fundamental and tax protection from general warranties; narrow the broad limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions.
5. **Fix disclosure and knowledge:** require fair, specific disclosure and remove constructive or discoverable knowledge.
6. **Complete verification:** check title and Completion deliverables; action the lease notice and review Mossvale without assuming a consent is needed.

These recommendations are based on the Seller’s summary and disclosure letter, not the complete SPA or underlying DD documents. The final mark-up should be checked against those documents and the deal record, particularly for conflicting definitions, actual contractual conditions and any genuinely agreed commercial positions.
